facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy
facts.text: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is named for a Japanese octopus trap, because the ballooned left ventricular apex with a narrow base resembles the jar. Hikaru Sato described it in 1990. It usually follows a physical or emotional stressor, mostly affects postmenopausal women, and the dysfunction is typically transient.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Bezold–Jarisch reflex
facts.text: The Bezold–Jarisch reflex is a vagally mediated triad of bradycardia, hypotension and hypopnea. Von Bezold and Hirt first saw it in 1867 after injecting Veratrum alkaloids, making it the first recognized chemical reflex. Severe hypovolemia or myocardial ischemia can also trigger it.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Brugada syndrome
facts.text: Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmia disorder with coved ST elevation in leads V1 to V3, yet only about 20% of cases involve SCN5A. Dangerous rhythms often occur at rest or during sleep, and in Thailand and Laos it is a leading cause of sudden death in otherwise healthy young men.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Eisenmenger syndrome
facts.text: In Eisenmenger syndrome, a long-standing left-to-right shunt such as a ventricular septal defect drives pulmonary hypertension until the shunt reverses to right-to-left and causes cyanosis. Victor Eisenmenger described it in 1897, and Paul Wood later gave it his name.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Kounis syndrome
facts.text: Kounis syndrome is acute coronary syndrome triggered by an allergic or hypersensitivity reaction. Mast cell mediators such as histamine and proteases can provoke coronary spasm or plaque rupture. Nicholas Kounis gave the first full description, in 1991.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Torsades de pointes
facts.text: Torsades de pointes is French for 'twisting of the points,' describing how the QRS complexes seem to twist around the baseline. François Dessertenne coined the term in 1966 after seeing it in an 80-year-old woman with intermittent complete AV block. It is classically linked to a prolonged QT interval.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Ventricular assist device
facts.text: Patients with continuous-flow left ventricular assist devices can have a greatly reduced or even absent pulse, because the rotary pump moves blood steadily rather than in beats. Liotta and Crawford implanted the first LVAD in 1963; Liotta and DeBakey achieved the first successful implantation in 1966.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Artificial heart valve
facts.text: The Starr-Edwards caged-ball valve, with a silicone ball inside a cage, was first implanted by Albert Starr in 1960. It remained in use for 47 years until it was retired in 2007, and one valve is reported to have lasted 48 years.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Bainbridge reflex
facts.text: The Bainbridge reflex raises heart rate when the right atrium is stretched by increased venous return. In 1915 Francis Bainbridge infused blood or saline into anesthetized dogs and saw tachycardia that vanished when the vagus was cut. The response depends on the baseline heart rate.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Bioactive glass
facts.text: Bioactive glass, developed by Larry Hench's group at the University of Florida starting in 1969, bonds to bone because its surface converts into a calcium phosphate layer that matures into hydroxyapatite, onto which bone grows. The best-known composition is 45S5, trademarked as Bioglass.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Alpha-gal syndrome
facts.text: Alpha-gal syndrome is an IgE-mediated allergy to the carbohydrate galactose-α-1,3-galactose found in mammalian meat. Unlike most food allergies, reactions typically begin 2 to 8 hours after eating. It is acquired after tick bites, and was uncovered when reactions to cetuximab led Thomas Platts-Mills's team to the same antibody.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Original antigenic sin
facts.text: Original antigenic sin is the tendency of the immune system to reuse memory from a first infection when it meets a drifted variant of a pathogen, which can blunt a fresh response. Thomas Francis Jr. coined it in 1960 from influenza work, as a play on the theological idea of original sin.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Microchimerism
facts.text: Microchimerism means carrying a small number of cells from another individual. After pregnancy, fetal cells can persist in the mother for decades; one study found male fetal cells in maternal blood 27 years later. Their health effects, including in autoimmune disease, remain unclear.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Biofilm
facts.text: Biofilms are microbial communities embedded in a self-made matrix of polysaccharides, proteins and DNA. Cells inside can tolerate antibiotics at levels far above those that kill free-floating cells, and biofilms often form on implanted devices such as catheters and prosthetic heart valves.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Refeeding syndrome
facts.text: Refeeding syndrome is a metabolic disturbance that follows restoring nutrition in a starved person. Returning insulin drives cells to take up phosphate, potassium and magnesium that are already depleted, so serum phosphate falls and ATP stores drop. It was probably first identified during the 1944–45 Dutch famine.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Theralizumab
facts.text: In March 2006, six healthy volunteers at a London phase 1 trial received TGN1412, a CD28 superagonist antibody, at about 1/500 of the highest dose given to macaques. All six were hospitalized within about 16 hours with severe cytokine release. Macaque effector memory T cells lack CD28, which explains why animal tests missed the risk.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Nickel titanium
facts.text: Nitinol's name combines nickel, titanium and the Naval Ordnance Laboratory, where William Buehler's team was seeking fatigue-resistant alloys for missile nose cones. Its shape memory and superelasticity let a collapsed stent spring back to its expanded shape once warmed to body temperature.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Immune privilege
facts.text: Immune privilege shields tissues such as the eye, testis and fetus from damaging immune responses. Mechanisms include limited lymphatic drainage, low MHC expression and constitutive Fas ligand, which restricts entry of Fas-expressing lymphocytes. In the eye, anterior chamber–associated immune deviation actively suppresses systemic responses.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 长城
facts.text: 长城很长，是中国古代的人建的，为了保护国家。
facts.translation: The Great Wall is very long. People in ancient China built it to protect the country.
facts.reading: Chángchéng hěn cháng, shì Zhōngguó gǔdài de rén jiàn de, wèile bǎohù guójiā.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 大熊猫
facts.text: 大熊猫几乎只吃竹子，大部分住在中国的四川。
facts.translation: Giant pandas eat almost only bamboo, and most of them live in Sichuan, China.
facts.reading: Dà xióngmāo jīhū zhǐ chī zhúzi, dà bùfen zhù zài Zhōngguó de Sìchuān.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 故宫
facts.text: 故宫在北京，是明朝和清朝皇帝住的地方，1420年建好。
facts.translation: The Forbidden City is in Beijing. It is where the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties lived, and it was finished in 1420.
facts.reading: Gùgōng zài Běijīng, shì Míngcháo hé Qīngcháo huángdì zhù de dìfang, 1420 nián jiàn hǎo.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 春节
facts.text: 春节是农历新年，除夕晚上，一家人在一起吃团圆饭。
facts.translation: The Spring Festival is the lunar new year. On New Year's Eve, the whole family eats a reunion dinner together.
facts.reading: Chūnjié shì nónglì xīnnián, chúxī wǎnshang, yījiārén zài yìqǐ chī tuányuánfàn.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 黄河
facts.text: 黄河是中国第二长的河，河水里有很多泥沙，所以是黄色的。
facts.translation: The Yellow River is the second longest river in China. Its water has a lot of silt, so it is yellow.
facts.reading: Huánghé shì Zhōngguó dì-èr cháng de hé, héshuǐ lǐ yǒu hěn duō níshā, suǒyǐ shì huángsè de.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 造纸术
facts.text: 造纸术是中国的四大发明之一，人们说汉代的蔡伦让造纸更好了。
facts.translation: Papermaking is one of China's Four Great Inventions. People say Cai Lun of the Han dynasty made papermaking better.
facts.reading: Zàozhǐshù shì Zhōngguó de sì dà fāmíng zhī yī, rénmen shuō Hàndài de Cài Lún ràng zàozhǐ gèng hǎo le.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 珠穆朗玛峰
facts.text: 珠穆朗玛峰是世界上最高的山，在中国和尼泊尔中间，高八千八百多米。
facts.translation: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain in the world. It is between China and Nepal and is over 8,800 meters high.
facts.reading: Zhūmùlǎngmǎ Fēng shì shìjiè shàng zuì gāo de shān, zài Zhōngguó hé Níbó'ěr zhōngjiān, gāo bāqiān bābǎi duō mǐ.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 中秋节
facts.text: 中秋节在农历八月十五，这一天人们常常吃月饼。
facts.translation: The Mid-Autumn Festival is on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, and people often eat mooncakes on this day.
facts.reading: Zhōngqiūjié zài nónglì bāyuè shíwǔ, zhè yì tiān rénmen chángcháng chī yuèbǐng.

facts.subject: mandarin
facts.title: 茶
facts.text: 茶是用茶树的叶子做的饮料，最早出现在中国。
facts.translation: Tea is a drink made from tea plant leaves, and it first appeared in China.
facts.reading: Chá shì yòng cháshù de yèzi zuò de yǐnliào, zuì zǎo chūxiàn zài Zhōngguó.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction
facts.text: In the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction, a mixture's color cycles repeatedly between yellow and colorless as cerium ion ratios oscillate. Boris Belousov found it in 1951, but journals rejected his paper because he could not explain it, and Western scientists only learned of the work around 1968.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Natural nuclear fission reactor
facts.text: About 1.7 billion years ago, uranium ore at Oklo in Gabon sustained natural fission, with groundwater slowing neutrons and then boiling away to pause the reaction in cycles of roughly three hours. It was discovered in 1972 when French analysts found the ore's uranium-235 content was 0.60% instead of 0.72%.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Hanny's Voorwerp
facts.text: Hanny's Voorwerp is a glowing gas cloud about the size of a small galaxy, spotted in 2007 by Dutch teacher Hanny van Arkel while volunteering for Galaxy Zoo. It is thought to be a quasar ionization echo, lit by a past burst from nearby galaxy IC 2497, whose quasar appears to have since switched off.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Lake Nyos
facts.text: On 21 August 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon suddenly released a huge cloud of carbon dioxide that suffocated 1,746 people and about 3,500 livestock within roughly 25 km. A degassing pipe installed in 2001 now siphons gas-rich water from the depths, with two more pipes added in 2011.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Hoatzin
facts.text: The hoatzin, a bird of the Amazon and Orinoco basins, digests leaves by bacterial fermentation in an enlarged two-chambered crop, much like a cow, which is unique among birds. Its strong smell earned it the name 'stinkbird', and its chicks have working claws on their wings for climbing.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Welwitschia
facts.text: Welwitschia, a plant of the Namib Desert, grows only two permanent leaves, which keep growing from the base for its entire life and can reach about 4 m. Many individuals are hundreds of years old, and the oldest may be close to 2,000.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Brinicle
facts.text: A brinicle is a hollow tube of ice that grows downward under forming sea ice, built around a plume of cold, very salty brine that sinks and freezes the seawater around it. If it reaches the seafloor, the brine can spread out and trap animals such as starfish and sea urchins. It was first filmed in 2011 for the BBC series Frozen Planet.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: War of the Bucket
facts.text: The 1325 War of the Bucket between Modena and Bologna ended at the Battle of Zappolino, a Modenese victory over a much larger Bolognese army. The wooden bucket of the name was taken as a trophy afterward; the war actually began after Modena captured the castle of Monteveglio.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Cod Wars
facts.text: Iceland and the UK clashed over fishing limits in three Cod Wars between 1958 and 1976, as Iceland pushed its zone out to 12, then 50, then 200 nautical miles. Coast guard ships cut trawl wires, ships rammed each other, and Iceland threatened to leave NATO before a 1976 deal gave it the 200-mile zone.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Lycurgus Cup
facts.text: The Lycurgus Cup, a Late Roman glass vessel, looks green in reflected light but glows red when light shines through it. The effect comes from gold and silver nanoparticles about 70 nm wide dispersed in the glass. It is kept in the British Museum.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Codex Seraphinianus
facts.text: Codex Seraphinianus is an illustrated encyclopedia of an imaginary world, made by Luigi Serafini in 1976–78 and published in 1981. Its text is in an invented script that Serafini says carries no meaning, though researchers worked out that its page numbers use a base-21 system.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Derinkuyu underground city
facts.text: Derinkuyu in Turkey's Cappadocia is an underground city reaching about 85 m deep that could shelter up to 20,000 people along with livestock. Rolling stone doors could seal each floor from inside, and the city was rediscovered in 1963 when a resident knocked through a basement wall.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Glass harmonica
facts.text: Benjamin Franklin built the glass harmonica in 1761 after hearing tuned wine glasses played; his version had 37 rotating glass bowls touched with wet fingers. Legends say it drove players mad, but how far that belief went is conjecture. Mozart wrote for it in 1791.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Silbo Gomero
facts.text: Silbo Gomero is a whistled form of Spanish used on La Gomera in the Canary Islands, able to carry messages across ravines up to about five kilometres. It has been taught in local schools since 1999, and UNESCO recognized it as intangible heritage in 2009.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Dazzle camouflage
facts.text: Dazzle camouflage, credited to artist Norman Wilkinson in World War I, did not try to hide ships. Its bold geometric patterns aimed to make it hard to judge a ship's range, speed and heading. Its effectiveness stayed uncertain; a 1918 Admiralty analysis was inconclusive.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Falkirk Wheel
facts.text: The Falkirk Wheel in Scotland is a rotating boat lift that raises boats 24 metres between two canals. Its water-filled gondolas always weigh the same, because a floating boat displaces its own weight in water, so each half-turn uses only about 1.5 kWh.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Beach Pneumatic Transit
facts.text: In 1870 Alfred Ely Beach opened a pneumatic subway under New York's Broadway: a single car blown through a tunnel about 300 feet long by air pressure. He first framed it as a postal tube project to get around Boss Tweed's opposition. It carried over 400,000 riders before closing in 1873.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Benford's law
facts.text: Benford's law says that in many real-world datasets the leading digit 1 appears about 30.1% of the time, while 9 leads under 5%. Simon Newcomb spotted it in 1881 from worn early pages of logarithm tables, and Frank Benford tested it in 1938. It is used as a screening tool in fraud detection.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Garum
facts.text: Garum was a fermented fish sauce prized in the Roman world, made by fermenting fish innards in salt and brine, in good conditions in about 48 hours. It was a major export from Hispania, and the production of Aulus Umbricius Scaurus was important to Pompeii's economy.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Project Orion (nuclear propulsion)
facts.text: Project Orion studied a spacecraft pushed along by nuclear explosions set off behind a pusher plate. Ted Taylor led it at General Atomics, with Freeman Dyson joining; the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty helped end it in 1964. Small models were flown with chemical explosives.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Pirahã language
facts.text: Pirahã, spoken by roughly 250–380 people along the Maici River in Brazil, is one of the phonologically simplest languages known, with as few as ten phonemes, and it can be whistled or hummed. Daniel Everett's claim that it lacks number words and recursion is disputed by many linguists.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Sonoluminescence
facts.text: Sonoluminescence is light emitted when bubbles in a liquid collapse under sound waves. It was first seen in 1934 by researchers studying sonar, and a single stable bubble was trapped in 1990. Each flash lasts only picoseconds, and the mechanism is still unknown.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Morning Glory cloud
facts.text: The Morning Glory is a roll cloud up to 1,000 km long that forms over northern Australia's Gulf of Carpentaria, the only place it can be reliably predicted. It travels at about 10 to 20 metres per second, and glider pilots gather at Burketown to ride the wave.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Fordlândia
facts.text: In 1928 Henry Ford founded Fordlândia, a planned town on Brazil's Tapajós River, to supply rubber for his cars. Poor soil, closely planted trees prone to blight, and worker unrest over imposed rules doomed it; in 1945 the company sold the land back to Brazil at a loss of over US$20 million.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Las Médulas
facts.text: Las Médulas, en León, fue la mayor mina de oro a cielo abierto del Imperio romano. Los romanos usaban la técnica de la «ruina montium»: soltaban mucha agua para deshacer la montaña. Es Patrimonio de la Humanidad desde 1997.
facts.translation: Las Médulas, in León, was the largest open-pit gold mine of the Roman Empire. The Romans used the 'ruina montium' technique: they released a lot of water to break down the mountain. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1997.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Caminito del Rey
facts.text: El Caminito del Rey es una pasarela en las paredes del desfiladero de los Gaitanes, en Málaga. Se construyó entre 1901 y 1905 para los trabajadores de unas centrales hidroeléctricas. Algunos tramos cuelgan hasta 105 metros sobre el río. Reabrió en 2015.
facts.translation: The Caminito del Rey is a walkway on the walls of the Gaitanes gorge, in Málaga. It was built between 1901 and 1905 for workers at hydroelectric plants. Some sections hang up to 105 meters above the river. It reopened in 2015.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Quilotoa
facts.text: Quilotoa es un volcán de Ecuador. Su caldera tiene una laguna de unos 250 metros de profundidad y de agua verde esmeralda. Hace unos 800 años tuvo una gran erupción, y hoy la caldera mide unos tres kilómetros.
facts.translation: Quilotoa is a volcano in Ecuador. Its caldera holds a lake about 250 meters deep with emerald-green water. About 800 years ago it had a huge eruption, and today the caldera is about three kilometers wide.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Palmeral de Elche
facts.text: El Palmeral de Elche, en Alicante, es el palmeral más grande de Europa, con entre 200 000 y 300 000 palmeras, sobre todo datileras. La UNESCO lo declaró Patrimonio de la Humanidad en el año 2000.
facts.translation: The Palmeral of Elche, in Alicante, is the largest palm grove in Europe, with between 200,000 and 300,000 palms, mostly date palms. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 2000.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Cueva de las Manos
facts.text: La Cueva de las Manos, en la Patagonia argentina, tiene cientos de siluetas de manos en las paredes. Se cree que el pigmento se soplaba con huesos huecos de animales. Las pinturas tienen miles de años, y la UNESCO la declaró Patrimonio de la Humanidad en 1999.
facts.translation: The Cave of the Hands, in Argentine Patagonia, has hundreds of hand outlines on its walls. It is believed the pigment was blown through hollow animal bones. The paintings are thousands of years old, and UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1999.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Castell
facts.text: Los castells son torres humanas de varios pisos que se construyen en las fiestas de Cataluña. El «enxaneta» sube hasta arriba y levanta un brazo para terminar la torre. La UNESCO los declaró Patrimonio Cultural Inmaterial de la Humanidad en 2010.
facts.translation: Castells are human towers of several levels built at festivals in Catalonia. The 'enxaneta' climbs to the top and raises an arm to finish the tower. UNESCO declared them Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Cenote Sagrado
facts.text: El Cenote Sagrado es un gran pozo natural de agua en Chichén Itzá, México, de unos 60 metros de diámetro. Los mayas lo usaron para ofrendas y sacrificios. En 1904 Edward Thompson empezó a dragarlo y sacó muchos objetos del país de forma ilegal.
facts.translation: The Sacred Cenote is a large natural water pit at Chichén Itzá, Mexico, about 60 meters across. The Maya used it for offerings and sacrifices. In 1904 Edward Thompson began dredging it and illegally took many objects out of the country.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Valle de Cocora
facts.text: El Valle de Cocora, en Colombia, es el hogar principal de la palma de cera del Quindío, el árbol nacional del país. Está en los Andes, entre 1800 y 2400 metros de altura.
facts.translation: The Cocora Valley, in Colombia, is the main home of the Quindío wax palm, the national tree of the country. It is in the Andes, between 1,800 and 2,400 meters high.

facts.subject: spanish
facts.title: Sima de los Huesos
facts.text: En la Sima de los Huesos, en Atapuerca, se encontraron restos de al menos 28 personas de hace unos 430 000 años. Los científicos creen que eran primeros neandertales. Allí también apareció un bifaz llamado «Excalibur», quizá una ofrenda.
facts.translation: In the Sima de los Huesos, in Atapuerca, the remains of at least 28 people from about 430,000 years ago were found. Scientists believe they were early Neanderthals. A hand axe called 'Excalibur' was also found there, perhaps an offering.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Tin pest
facts.text: Below 13.2 °C, metallic white tin can slowly turn into brittle grey tin with a diamond-cubic structure. The change expands the metal by about 27%, so objects crumble, and once started it accelerates on its own. Medieval church organ pipes were hit as early as 1467.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Gakkel Ridge
facts.text: The Gakkel Ridge under the Arctic Ocean spreads at under 1 cm a year, the slowest known spreading ridge. Even so, a 2007 expedition found pyroclastic deposits over 10 km² of its axial valley, with volatile levels about ten times normal for such ridges.

facts.subject: random
facts.title: Tritone paradox
facts.text: Play two tones exactly half an octave apart, built from stacked octaves, and listeners disagree on whether the pair rises or falls. Diana Deutsch found in 1986 that the answer depends on the listener's speech background: Californians and southern English speakers resolve it in opposite ways.

facts.subject: cardiology
facts.title: Naxos disease
facts.text: On the Greek island of Naxos, doctors described a family syndrome that links woolly hair and thick palms and soles with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. A 2000 study traced it to a plakoglobin deletion, a desmosome protein. Up to 1 in 1,000 islanders is affected.

facts.subject: medicine
facts.title: Osseointegration
facts.text: Titanium screws in rat femurs tightened over 6 to 16 weeks in Leventhal's 1951 work, which predates Brånemark. In 1952 Brånemark's titanium chamber in rabbit bone fused so completely that it could not be removed. He coined the term, and in 1965 placed the first human dental implant.
